word:greek-nt:G0055.explanation: This word means “purely,” describing something done with an unmixed or sincere quality rather than with a hidden mixture of motives. It functions as a concise description of how an action is carried out. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Philippians 1:17. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the specific action or motive being described there, but the word itself points to purity in the manner or intention involved.

word:greek-nt:G0107.explanation: Azor is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears twice, in Matthew 1:13 and Matthew 1:14. The English Bible preserves it as “Azor,” so its meaning is chiefly its identity as the person named. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain Azor’s specific role in either passage.

word:greek-nt:G0172.explanation: Akakos means innocent or simple. It can also mean guileless, describing someone as blameless.

word:greek-nt:G0240.explanation: Allēlōn means one another or each other. It marks an action shared between people, such as loving one another.

word:greek-nt:G0341.explanation: Anakainō means to renew or make new again.

word:greek-nt:G0503.explanation: This Greek word means “to face” or “to head into.” It describes directing oneself toward something rather than turning away from it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:15, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word presents forward movement or direct confrontation with what lies ahead, while the exact English wording may vary according to context. Its central idea remains meeting or moving toward something directly.

word:greek-nt:G0657.explanation: Apotassō means to take leave. It can also mean sending someone away or renouncing what one has. It may describe saying goodbye.

word:greek-nt:G0734.explanation: Artemas is a personal name, referring to a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name occurs once and is rendered “Artemas.” Its single occurrence is in Titus 3:12. The name itself supplies identification, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain Artemas’s role in that specific setting of Paul’s letter.

word:greek-nt:G0789.explanation: Assos is a port of Mysia in the Roman province of Asia.

word:greek-nt:G0860.explanation: This word means a “joint” or “ligament”—a connecting part of the body that joins separate members together. It is used as a bodily term in the Greek New Testament, appearing twice, in Ephesians 4:16 and Colossians 2:19. Its central idea is connection: parts are joined through such members, allowing the body to be understood as an ordered, united whole. The precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G0994.explanation: Boao means to shout, call aloud, or cry out.

word:greek-nt:G1063.explanation: Gar means “for,” linking a statement to the reason or explanation that follows.

word:greek-nt:G1166.explanation: Deiknyō means to point out, show, or make something known.

word:greek-nt:G1188.explanation: Dexios means right, including the right-hand side or right hand.

word:greek-nt:G1261.explanation: Dialogismos means a thought. It can also describe reasoning.

word:greek-nt:G1430.explanation: Dōma means the roof or top of a house—the housetop.

word:greek-nt:G1719.explanation: Emphobos means full of fear—afraid or terrified.

word:greek-nt:G1801.explanation: Enōtizomai means to listen carefully or give ear to what is said.

word:greek-nt:G1896.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “to look upon” and can also express “to show favor.” It describes directing attention toward someone, with the added sense that the person being viewed receives gracious regard. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 1:25 and Acts 4:29. Its exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central idea joins looking with purposeful, favorable attention rather than merely seeing something incidentally.

word:greek-nt:G1944.explanation: Epikataratos means cursed—under a curse or accursed.

word:greek-nt:G2017.explanation: This word means “to shine on,” describing light appearing or being directed upon something. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Ephesians 5:14. Its basic sense concerns the arrival or giving of light; the surrounding verse determines the precise force of that action in context.

word:greek-nt:G2062.explanation: Herpeton means a creeping creature, especially a reptile.

word:greek-nt:G2206.explanation: Zēloō means to be jealous of a person or to desire something eagerly. The word can describe jealousy against Joseph and earnest desire for spiritual gifts.

word:greek-nt:G2291.explanation: Thara is the name of Terah, Abraham’s father.

word:greek-nt:G2343.explanation: Thēsaurizō means to store up, treasure up, save, or lay up. It can describe laying up treasure or treasuring up wrath.

word:greek-nt:G2413.explanation: Hieros means sacred, holy, or set apart. It can also refer to a temple.

word:greek-nt:G2725.explanation: This word means “accusers”—people who bring charges or allegations against another person. It describes those presenting a case against someone, rather than the person defending himself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Acts, where it consistently refers to people bringing accusations before authorities. The central idea is therefore a person or group acting as a claimant against someone in a legal or formal complaint.

word:greek-nt:G2783.explanation: Kēryx means a herald or proclaimer who announces a message. It also describes a preacher, as Noah is called a preacher of righteousness.

word:greek-nt:G2826.explanation: Klinidion means a couch or bed for a sick person.

word:greek-nt:G2967.explanation: Kōlyō means to prevent, hinder, or keep someone from doing something. It can describe blocking people from entering or keeping someone from being baptized.

word:greek-nt:G3050.explanation: Logikos means reasonable or rational. It can also be rendered spiritual.

word:greek-nt:G3087.explanation: Lychnia means a lamp-stand, a stand where a lamp is placed so its light can be seen.

word:greek-nt:G3173.explanation: Megas means large or great in a broad sense.

word:greek-nt:G3432.explanation: Moichos means an adulterer, a man guilty with a married woman.

word:greek-nt:G3447.explanation: This word means “to make a calf” or “to make an idol in the shape of a calf.” It describes the act of producing a calf-shaped idol, not merely seeing or possessing one. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 7:41, in connection with the making of the calf. Its meaning is therefore specific: creating an object of worship fashioned in a calf’s likeness.

word:greek-nt:G3490.explanation: This Greek New Testament word refers to a ship’s “captain” or “ship owner”—the person responsible for the vessel. It is a specific term rather than a broad word for any sailor or passenger. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 27:11, so its normal meaning is clear, while the precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G3515.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means to be childlike or to be a child. It describes a person’s condition or manner rather than naming a specific object. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 1 Corinthians 14:20. Its basic sense is clear, while the surrounding verse and passage determine exactly how that childlike quality is being addressed there.

word:greek-nt:G3609.explanation: Oiketeia means household or family members—those belonging to a household. It can describe the household of faith.

word:greek-nt:G3700.explanation: Optanomai means to appear or to be seen by others.

word:greek-nt:G3865.explanation: Paratheōreō means to overlook or neglect.

word:greek-nt:G3911.explanation: Parapherō means to carry away or remove.

word:greek-nt:G3968.explanation: Patris means a fatherland or one's native place, including a hometown.

word:greek-nt:G3986.explanation: Peirasmos means a trial. It can also refer to temptation.

word:greek-nt:G4015.explanation: Periastrapto means to flash or shine around like lightning.

word:greek-nt:G4147.explanation: Plouteō means to be rich or to become rich.

word:greek-nt:G4190.explanation: Ponēros means evil, bad, wicked, or malicious. It can describe evil thoughts or a wicked servant.

word:greek-nt:G4200.explanation: Porismos means a source of gain or livelihood.

word:greek-nt:G4309.explanation: Proorizo means to foreordain or predetermine, marking something out beforehand.

word:greek-nt:G4473.explanation: Rhantismos means sprinkling. It can also mean purification.

word:greek-nt:G4550.explanation: Sapros means rotten or corrupt. It can also describe what is bad.

word:greek-nt:G4587.explanation: Semnotēs means dignity and seriousness in conduct. It is used for gravity in household conduct and seriousness in teaching.

word:greek-nt:G4756.explanation: Stratia means an army or host. It can also refer to the heavenly host. In one passage, this host is a multitude praising God.

word:greek-nt:G4859.explanation: This word means “mutual consent” or “mutually consenting,” describing agreement reached willingly by the people involved. It emphasizes shared agreement rather than the decision or action of only one person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 7:5. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: both parties agree together before something takes place.

word:greek-nt:G4998.explanation: Sōphrōn means self-controlled, sober-minded, or temperate.

word:greek-nt:G5085.explanation: Tiberias is the name of a town in Galilee. The Sea of Galilee is also called the Sea of Tiberias.

word:greek-nt:G5131.explanation: The word means a he-goat, that is, a male goat. It names the animal itself rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Hebrews 9–10. The word therefore keeps a concrete, ordinary meaning: a male goat being discussed in the passage. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding context.

word:greek-nt:G5148.explanation: This word means “three years,” referring to a period lasting three complete years. It expresses a measure of time rather than an event, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 20:31. Its exact significance in that verse is understood from the surrounding sentence and passage, but the word itself simply identifies the length of the period as three years.

word:greek-nt:G5229.explanation: Hyperairō means to raise beyond or exalt oneself. It can describe arrogant or conceited self-exaltation, such as exalting oneself above all that is called God.

word:greek-nt:G5294.explanation: Hypotithēmi means to lay down and can describe risking oneself. It can also mean to put something in mind or teach it.

word:greek-nt:G5360.explanation: Philadelphia means brotherly love, love among Christian brethren.

word:greek-nt:G5416.explanation: Phragellion means a scourge or whip.

word:greek-nt:G5481.explanation: This Greek New Testament word describes an “exact representation” or “reproduction”—something that corresponds precisely to what it represents. It emphasizes exact likeness rather than a loose resemblance, making it useful for describing an image or expression that faithfully reflects its original. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Hebrews 1:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G5579.explanation: Pseudos means a lie, falsehood, or untruth.

word:greek-nt:G6008.explanation: This word means “jump up.” It describes a sudden upward movement and functions as an action word, presenting someone as rising or springing upward. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:50. That single occurrence supports a focused meaning rather than a broad range of uses: the word points to the act of jumping up itself. The surrounding verse determines who performs the action and why, but the word’s basic sense remains a physical upward movement.

word:greek-nt:G6071.explanation: This word means “further,” expressing an extension beyond what has already been said or reached. It is a Greek New Testament word that appears once, at Acts 19:39. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, its exact force in that sentence cannot be described more specifically. Its basic role is to indicate continuation or additional scope.
